back: Anything applied to, or done to, a material's surface to protect it, improve its appearance, or both.
They stop ferrous metals rusting, stop timber absorbing moisture and rotting, protect polymers from UV and scratches, and make products hygienic and hard-wearing.
They add colour, change texture and sheen (gloss, satin, matt), and enhance or hide natural features such as grain.
Clean off rust, grease and scale with emery cloth, wire wool or degreaser; some finishes need the surface keyed (roughened).
Electrostatically charged polymer powder is sprayed onto metal, then baked so it melts into a hard, even, chip-resistant coat — bike frames, garden furniture.
Heated metal (about 200°C) is dipped into a fluidised bed of polythene powder, which melts on, then cured — soft, grippy and insulating, e.g. tool handles.
The first coat on bare material — seals the surface, prevents corrosion on metal and helps the top coat stick.

front: Why does paint on bare steel fail?
back: Without a metal primer it soon flakes and the steel rusts underneath.
A clear or tinted coating that dries into a hard, waterproof layer showing the grain; applied in thin coats, sanded lightly between.
Rubbed in and buffed to a soft sheen — enhances the grain but gives little protection against water or heat and needs reapplying.
Seals the pores of the wood before varnish, wax or paint so fewer top coats are needed.

front: Why must MDF be primed or sealed before painting?
back: Its cut edges are very absorbent, so paint would soak in.

front: How are manufactured boards usually finished?
back: Painted, veneered or covered with a laminate such as melamine, because they have no attractive grain.
Sand with progressively finer grades, remove dust, apply sealer or primer, lightly sand, then thin top coats with light sanding between.
A material that comes out of manufacture with its final colour, texture and surface, so it needs no applied finish.
Colour runs all the way through, the mould gives the surface texture or gloss, and they do not corrode.
Draw filing, wet-and-dry paper (used wet), polishing compound, or flame polishing on acrylic.
